# 7.2.1 — Time Generated by Soul: *Enneads* III.7

---

## The Central Passage

The most important passage in Plotinus's philosophy of time is *Enneads* III.7.11, where he offers his own positive account of what time is, after critiquing the alternatives. The key sentence is: "Time is the life of the Soul in a movement of passage from one way of life to another" (*Enneads* III.7.11.43–45, trans. Armstrong 1967). This sentence is compressed but precise, and unpacking it takes us to the heart of Plotinus's view.

The sentence does not say that time is measured by Soul, or that Soul is aware of time, or that time depends on Soul for its measurement. It says that time *is* the life of Soul in its particular mode of activity — the mode of "passage from one way of life to another." Time is not a container in which Soul lives; it is the form of Soul's living. Soul does not move through time as a fish moves through water; Soul *is* temporal because its mode of being is essentially sequential and transitional.

## Why Soul Generates Time

To understand why Plotinus thinks Soul generates time, we need to understand what Soul is trying to do and why it cannot do it all at once.

Soul proceeds from Intellect and in some sense aspires to be like Intellect — to grasp all things in a single, undivided act. But Soul cannot do this. Its mode of being is discursive (*dianoêtikos*): it must move from thought to thought, from one activity to another, building up its understanding sequentially. Where Intellect knows all Forms simultaneously and completely, Soul knows them one after another — or rather, it presents them to itself in a sequence that is the temporal unfolding of what Intellect grasps all at once.

Plotinus uses the image of a restless soul that cannot remain still: "Soul was not willing to remain with Intellect but wanted to possess all it had in itself in another manner" (*Enneads* III.7.11.16–18, trans. Armstrong 1967). This "wanting to possess in another manner" is the root of time. Soul, by its nature, generates a series — it cannot hold everything at once, so it unfolds everything in succession. That unfolding is time.

## The Analogy of the Seed and the Tree

Plotinus offers an analogy that illuminates this account. Consider a seed: it contains, in some sense, the entire structure of the tree it will become — roots, trunk, branches, leaves, fruit. But this content is not all present simultaneously in the seed in the way it will be present in the mature tree. The seed "unfolds" what is implicit in it through a process of temporal development. 

Intellect is like the tree: its entire content is present simultaneously, completely actualized. Soul is like the seed in the process of growing: its content is genuine, but it can only be actualized sequentially, through a temporal process. Time is the "growing" by which Soul actualizes what it contains (*Enneads* III.7.11.1–15, trans. Armstrong 1967).

This analogy makes clear why Plotinus's account is neither a simple idealism (time as a product of individual human minds) nor a simple realism (time as an independently existing feature of the physical world). Time is a feature of Soul — the cosmic Soul, not any individual human mind — and the physical world is temporal because it is animated by this cosmic Soul. Individual human temporal experience is a participation in the cosmic Soul's temporal activity.

## The Character of Soul's Temporal Life

What exactly is the "movement of passage from one way of life to another" that Plotinus identifies with time? Soul moves through its activities — its discursive thinking, its administration of the physical world, its care for individual souls — in a sequential manner. This sequencing is not arbitrary but ordered: each state of Soul follows from the previous state according to the rational principles (*logoi*) that govern Soul's activity. The sequence is thus the temporal "image" of the rational structure that Intellect grasps all at once.

This is an important feature of Plotinus's account. Time is not merely arbitrary succession; it is ordered succession, a rational sequence. The temporal order reflects the logical and ontological order that Intellect holds in its eternal grasp. Time is, in this sense, the temporal expression of the rational structure of being — it is what the logos looks like when it is encountered by a nature that must unfold it step by step.

## The Cosmic Dimension

Plotinus is not describing the time of individual human consciousness, though individual temporal experience is a participation in what he describes. He is describing the temporal life of the cosmic Soul — the principle that animates and orders the entire physical universe. Time, for Plotinus, is cosmic before it is personal.

This is different from what some readers expect when they first encounter Plotinus's phrase "time is the life of Soul." They expect a theory of temporal consciousness — a phenomenology of how time is experienced by individual minds. And Plotinus's account does have implications for individual temporal experience; but it is primarily a cosmological claim about the source and nature of time as a feature of the universe, not a phenomenological claim about how time appears to a particular subject.

Augustine will later do something closer to a pure phenomenology of time — attending to how individual consciousness structures temporal experience. Plotinus's account is both grander in scope (it covers the cosmic Soul, not just individual minds) and less phenomenologically fine-grained than Augustine's.
